processing: The rhizome of Rhodiola rosea is dried and cut; as is usual for roots, it is then steeped long or simmered rather than briefly infused.
harvest_season: Little is recorded for the tea itself; as with other medicinal roots, it is dug rather than picked, and sold dried year round.
appearance_dry: Woody rhizome pieces with the bronze, old-gilt surface that gave the plant its name, turning pinkish at a fresh cut.
appearance_liquor: Typical of steeped woody roots, a brownish amber; little is documented about this tea's cup specifically.
appearance_wet: Swollen woody chips, darker than when dry.
taste_profile: Few reliable tasting notes exist. The root itself smells of rose, and a woody, bitter edge is what you would expect from a steeped rhizome.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for woody roots, not an established recipe: steep covered or simmer gently, and begin with a weak cup.

vintage_note: Sold without vintage, as dried root by weight or in herbal mixes. As with other roots, there is no prized year or season for the buyer to chase; look for a clear botanical name, Rhodiola rosea, on the pack.
description:
Golden root is the dried rhizome of Rhodiola rosea, a perennial of the stonecrop family. The name comes from the rhizome's colour, bronze or old gilding with a pearly shine, and the plant's other Russian name, rose root, comes from its rose scent and pink cut surface.

It is a root drink, so handling differs from leaf tea: pieces need time and heat. As with other woody roots, a long covered steep or a gentle simmer is the usual approach.

Tasting notes are scarce. The rose smell of the root is the one thing to go on, and expect some bitterness and woodiness, as is common for roots. Start weak and adjust.

Buy by the Latin name, because the name golden root is loose and sellers tie it to more than one region. It is often sold as a medicinal herb, so treat any health claims on the pack with care.
history: Little is documented about golden root as an everyday drink. What is secure is the botany and the naming: the Russian names refer to the colour and rose-scented cut of the rhizome. No date or person can be given for when people began brewing it as tea.
